```python
import numpy as np

data = np.random.randn(30000, 28000)
pca_model = decomposition.PCA(0.95, whiten=True)
pca_model.fit(data)
```

issues.title: CountVectorizer fails when dealing with short strings and ngram_range > len of the strings
issues.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

I was debugging a problem with the skrub GapEncoder in https://github.com/skrub-data/skrub/issues/770, and I realized that the root of the problem is somewhere in the CountVectorizer, specifically when it receives a column that includes only strings of length 1 (`"A"`). 

After tracking down the problem, my understanding is that the CountVectorizer is failing because all strings in the column are shorter than the minimum value in `ngram_range` (see the example). 

The result is the exception
```
ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
```

which is not giving me a lot of information to debug. I think the error message could be improved so that it describes the situation in more detail. 

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
import string

rng = np.random.default_rng()
letters = rng.choice(list(string.ascii_letters), 1000)

# works
CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ).fit_transform(np.array(letters))
# raises ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ngram_range=(2,4)).fit_transform(np.array(letters))
```

### Expected Results

I think it makes sense that the exception is raised, so the current behavior is "expected". I would rather have a more informative error if possible, however. Something like "the vocabulary is empty because all values in the series are shorter than the minimum value of ngram_range".

issues.title: BUG: Explicit validation data does not enable HistGradientBoosting automatic early stopping
issues.body:
### Introduce yourself

Hello, I am using sklearn for the forecasting project and in the meantime found some issues I reported here. 

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

Keep `early_stopping=True` as a passing control. Additional coverage should preserve the sample-count rule when validation arrays are absent, including the 10,000-sample boundary, and preserve the existing validation-argument errors.

Related work: [#18748](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/18748) requested custom validation-set support, and [#27124](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27124) introduced the explicit validation arguments. These references do not establish that no duplicate report exists.

issues.title: BUG: Pipeline.fit_predict skips transform_input for final-step metadata
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With metadata routing enabled and `transform_input=["X_val"]`, `Pipeline.fit_predict` passes transformed training data to the final estimator but leaves `X_val` untransformed. An otherwise identical call to `Pipeline.fit` transforms `X_val` correctly.

In the reproducer, the final estimator receives `X_val = [[15.0]]` through `fit_predict`, although the fitted scaler maps that value to `[[0.0]]`. No exception is raised.

This can put training data and validation metadata in different feature spaces. An estimator that uses the metadata could therefore compute incorrect validation quantities or make different fitting decisions. Preprocessing that changes the feature count could instead cause a shape error. These are potential consequences; the reproducer demonstrates the incorrect metadata, not a production failure or incorrect predictions from a built-in estimator.

The [documented purpose of `transform_input`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html) is to transform selected metadata before the consuming step receives it, including validation data.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)


class RecordsXVal(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        self.X_val_seen_ = X_val
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.zeros(len(X))

    def fit_predict(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.

issues.title: DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis
issues.body:
### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a data scientist in Toronto working on forecasting and causal inference. I've recently started contributing to scikit-learn — I have an open PR at #34888 (array API support for ShrunkCovariance) — and I found this while looking into #33712, where I was trying to work out which of two distinct undefined cases in balanced_accuracy_score that issue refers to. This one turned out to be independent of it, so I'm filing it separately.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

balanced_accuracy_score(..., adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the internal NaN filter. The adjusted score is bounded — it spans [-1, 1], reaching -1 only at n_classes=2 — so -inf is outside the documented range of the metric.

This surfaces in cross-validation on small or imbalanced folds, where a fold can easily contain a single class. One -inf propagates through any mean over folds, turning the whole aggregate into -inf and silently destroying an otherwise valid CV score. The related nan case is at least absorbed by nan-aware aggregation; -inf is not.

Mechanism: n_classes is read after the NaN filter at _classification.py:2940, so when one class survives, chance = 1 / 1 and `score /= 1 - chance` at line 2946 divides by zero. The np.errstate guard wraps the per-class division only, not this one, and has been scoped that way since the original commit (e888c0d65cf, "ENH multiclass balanced accuracy" #10587, 2018) — the guard and the unguarded division were introduced together.

This is separate from #33712: it predates it and reproduces without touching replace_undefined_by.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

# Case 1
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], adjusted=True))

# Case 2
```

comments.body:
Confirmed reproducing on current `main`. The mechanism is exactly as described, and I traced it to the `adjusted` branch of `balanced_accuracy_score` in `sklearn/metrics/_classification.py`:

```python
with context_manager:
    per_class = xp.linalg.diagonal(C) / xp.sum(C, axis=1)
if xp.any(xp.isnan(per_class)):
    warnings.warn("y_pred contains classes not in y_true")
    per_class = per_class[~xp.isnan(per_class)]   # a single class can survive here
score = xp.mean(per_class)
if adjusted:
    n_classes = per_class.shape[0]               # == 1
    chance = 1 / n_classes                        # == 1
    score -= chance
    score /= 1 - chance                           # 1 - 1 == 0 -> division by zero -> -inf
```

Two details line up with what you found. `n_classes` is read from `per_class` *after* the NaN filter, so when a predicted class isn't present in `y_true`, its column is filtered out and a single class can remain, giving `chance = 1`. And the `np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore")` context manager wraps only the `per_class` division above — the `adjusted` arithmetic runs outside it, so `score /= 1 - chance` is unguarded and returns `-inf`. Unlike the `nan` case, `-inf` isn't absorbed by nan-aware aggregation, so one such fold collapses an entire CV mean.

Minimal repro (a class in `y_pred` absent from `y_true`, so the NaN filter leaves one class):

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

y_true = [0, 0, 0, 0]
y_pred = [0, 0, 1, 1]
print(balanced_accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred, adjusted=True))  # -inf
```

I'd be glad to implement the fix, but I don't want to pre-empt the return-value semantics for the single-class case, since — as you flagged — that choice interacts with the `replace_undefined_by` direction being discussed in #33712. Worth noting the perfectly-single-class case (e.g. `y_true == y_pred == [0, 0, 0]`) already returns `nan` via `0/0`, so `adjusted=True` currently has two distinct undefined paths that resolve differently; whatever's decided in #33712 may want to unify them. Once maintainers settle the intended behavior, I'm happy to put up a PR with a regression test covering both the `-inf` (NaN-filter) path and the CV-aggregation impact. Flagging for triage.

issues.title: Birch: subcluster radius is numerically unstable far from the origin — clustering is not translation-invariant
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**``Birch``**  derives each subcluster's squared radius from the **non-centered** second moment, `r² = Σᵢ‖xᵢ‖²/n − ‖c‖²` (`_CFSubcluster.merge_subcluster` in `sklearn/cluster/_birch.py`). Both terms scale like ‖offset‖², so far from the origin they are large and nearly equal, and their float64 difference loses the unit-scale variance to **catastrophic cancellation**. `r²` then reads noise (often negative → clamped to 0), so `threshold` no longer bounds the leaf radius and the CF-tree silently changes structure. Concretely, a **pure translation** of the input — which cannot change Birch's result in exact arithmetic — changes the number of subclusters.



### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.cluster import Birch

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = np.vstack([rng.randn(200, 2), rng.randn(200, 2) + [15.0, 0.0]])  # two tight blobs, spread ~1

base = len(Birch(threshold=1.0, n_clusters=None).fit(X).subcluster_centers_)
print(f"sklearn {sklearn.__version__}  baseline (offset 0): {base} subclusters")
for off in (1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8):
    n = len(Birch(threshold=1.0, n_clusters=None).fit(X + off).subcluster_centers_)
    print(f"  offset={off:.0e}: {n:4d}  {'OK' if n == base else 'DEGRADED'}")
```

### Expected Results

The subcluster count is invariant under translation (Birch's `threshold` test is translation-equivariant in exact arithmetic): `12` at every offset.

### Actual Results

```
sklearn 1.9.0  baseline (offset 0): 12 subclusters
  offset=1e+05:   12  OK
  offset=1e+06:   13  DEGRADED
  offset=1e+07:   11  DEGRADED
  offset=1e+08:   99  DEGRADED
```


### Versions

```shell

    python: 3.12.13 (main, Mar 24 2026, 22:49:22) [Clang 22.1.1 ]
   machine: Linux-7.0.14-201.fc44.x86_64-x86_64-with-glibc2.43

Python dependencies:

        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0

threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

    num_threads: 16

        version: 0.3.33.112.0
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: Haswell

       user_api: openmp
   internal_api: openmp
    num_threads: 16
         prefix: libgomp
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd be glad to work on the PR. The cancellation is in `new_ss / new_n − new_sq_norm`, from accumulating `squared_sum_` as raw `Σ‖x‖²`. The standard remedy: store the **centered** second moment `Σᵢ‖xᵢ − c‖²` and combine subclusters with the numerically stable **parallel-axis (Chan et al.) update** — the common offset cancels *before* squaring. With that (a Python-only change to `_birch.py`) the MRE stays exactly invariant through offset **1e7** (vs 1e6 today), a ~100× extension; `1e8` still degrades but less (66 vs 99) — the residual is the fundamental float64 limit (unit spread ≈ 10 ULP at 1e8), not the formula. This is the instability and fix documented in **BETULA** (Lang & Schubert, *"BETULA: Numerically Stable CF-Trees for BIRCH Clustering"*, SISAP 2020 / Information Systems 2021). Ready implementation in #34433 (closed pending this issue, per @virchan) — happy to re-submit once scope is agreed

issues.title: StratifiedGroupKFold returns an empty fold when n_groups == n_splits: least-populated-fold tiebreak is defeated by 1-ULP noise
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

`StratifiedGroupKFold` can return an empty test fold even when `n_groups >= n_splits`, because the "least populated fold" tiebreak in `_find_best_fold` is defeated by 1-ULP floating-point noise.

`_find_best_fold` selects a fold with:

```python
is_current_fold_better = fold_eval < min_eval or (
    np.isclose(fold_eval, min_eval)
    and samples_in_fold < min_samples_in_fold
)
```

The first branch uses an exact `<`. When two candidate folds are *mathematically* tied, `np.std` still returns values that differ by an ULP or two, so `fold_eval < min_eval` fires and that fold wins outright — the `samples_in_fold` comparison never runs. That comparison is the "heuristic for assigning group to the least populated fold in cases when all other criteria are equal" documented in the changelist comment at the top of `_iter_test_indices`, and in practice it is largely unreachable.

When `n_groups == n_splits` there is no slack: a single misdirected group leaves a fold with nothing in it.

This is distinct from #33085, which was about `n_groups < n_splits` and was addressed by #33176 (that PR was titled "Towards #33085" and the issue remains open).

**Impact.** `cross_val_score` silently produces `nan` for the empty fold, so the aggregate score becomes `nan`:

```python
scores: [0.6  0.375  nan  0.6]   ->  mean nan
```

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold

y = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0]  # 3 classes, 6 samples each
g = [0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 3, 3, 0, 2]  # 4 groups, sizes 5/3/2/8

for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=4).split(y, y, g)):
    print(f"fold {i}: n_train={len(tr):2d} n_test={len(te):2d}")
```

### Expected Results

Four non-empty test folds. With 4 groups and 4 splits the assignment is forced to one group per fold.

```
fold 0: n_train=16 n_test= 2
fold 1: n_train=15 n_test= 3
fold 2: n_train=13 n_test= 5
fold 3: n_train=10 n_test= 8
```

### Actual Results

```
fold 0: n_train=13 n_test= 5
fold 1: n_train=10 n_test= 8
fold 2: n_train=18 n_test= 0    <-- empty test fold
fold 3: n_train=13 n_test= 5
```

`shuffle` does not help: all 24 relabellings of the four groups, and all of `random_state=0..199` with `shuffle=True`, still produce an empty fold.

### Mechanism

Instrumenting the assignment loop, the second group is the decisive one:

```
-- group 1 counts=[0, 1, 2]
     fold 0: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 1: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 2: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 3: eval=0.12028130608117203  samples_before=2   <- 1 ULP lower
     -> chose fold 3
```

Three folds are empty, fold 3 already holds a group, and all four evaluations are mathematically identical. Fold 3 wins on a 1-ULP artefact, and fold 2 is never filled.

Measured over 15898 group-assignment decisions from randomised configurations:

- 7.0% of decisions have two or more mathematically tied folds whose winner is decided by floating-point noise (median deciding difference **1 ULP**, max 3).
- In 6.9% of all decisions the intended least-populated-fold tiebreak would have selected a *different* fold than the one actually chosen.

### Additional counterexamples

Found by random search; all reproduce identically on 1.9.0 and 1.10.dev0.

| `n_splits` | `n_groups` | `n` | fold sizes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 22 | `[6, 11, 0, 5]` |
| 6 | 6 | 24 | `[4, 6, 6, 0, 4, 4]` |
| 4 | 4 | 20 | `[4, 9, 0, 7]` |
| 5 | 5 | 13 | `[2, 3, 4, 0, 4]` |

Every failing case I found is at `n_groups == n_splits`; with one spare group I found none in ~25k configurations either way.

### Suggested fix

Require a strictly-better evaluation to be better by more than noise, so the tiebreak becomes reachable:

```python
is_tied = np.isclose(fold_eval, min_eval)
is_current_fold_better = (fold_eval < min_eval and not is_tied) or (
    is_tied and samples_in_fold < min_samples_in_fold
)
```

With that change the reproducer yields `[2, 3, 5, 8]`, and in a sweep of the sensitive regime (`n_splits` 2-6, `n_classes` 2-4, `n < 40`) empty folds go from **4/73401 to 0/73401**. `pytest --pyargs sklearn.model_selection` is unchanged at 642 passed / 238 skipped.

Two caveats worth discussing:

1. **It changes roughly 21% of splits.** That is the size of the latent defect rather than an over-aggressive tolerance: tightening `np.isclose` to `rtol=1e-9` or `1e-12` gives the same 21%, because these are true ties; exact equality drops churn to 0.3% but does not fix the bug.
2. **Stratification quality is essentially unchanged** — mean fold-size CV 0.2393 both ways, mean per-fold class-proportion deviation 0.10618 vs 0.10620 over 4000 configurations. This is a correctness fix for the degenerate case, not an improvement to stratification (cf. #24656).

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8]
   machine: macOS-26.6-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
        numpy: 2.6.0.dev0
        scipy: 2.0.0.dev0
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Also reproduced on released sklearn 1.9.0 with numpy 2.5.2 / scipy 1.18.1.
```

Hi @StefanieSenger,

Thanks for triaging this.

### On detecting empty folds

I agree that this is worth doing irrespective of the tiebreak decision. One important detail is that the `check_array` error already happens, but `cross_val_score` hides it because `error_score` has a default value set to `np.nan`. So the check would need to happen at the split level, before fitting each fold.

I don’t think this replaces the tiebreak fix, though. In this case, the data can be split into 4 non-empty folds. Therefore, raising would force the user to use fewer folds even though 4 is valid.

- empty-fold detection handles genuinely impossible splits
- tiebreak fix handles splits that should have worked but are being decided by floating-point noise.

issues.title: explained_variance_score returns a perfect 1.0 for a single sample (silently breaks LeaveOneOut CV)
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

`explained_variance_score` returns `1.0` (a perfect score) for a single sample no
matter how wrong the prediction is, and emits no warning. `r2_score`, its
documented sibling, guards the same degenerate case with an
`UndefinedMetricWarning` and returns `nan`.

With one sample there is no variance to explain, so the numerator
(`Var(y_true - y_pred)`) and the denominator (`Var(y_true)`) are both `0`, and
`force_finite` maps `0/0` to `1.0` — documented as "perfect predictions" — even
when the prediction is plainly wrong.

The practical consequence is that **`LeaveOneOut` cross-validation scored with
`explained_variance` silently reports a perfect 1.0 for any model, including one
fit on pure noise.**

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import explained_variance_score, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_score

# 1) single sample, clearly wrong prediction
print(explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]))  # 1.0, no warning
print(r2_score([1.0], [2.0]))                  # nan + UndefinedMetricWarning

# 2) the practical impact: LeaveOneOut on pure noise
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X, y = rng.normal(size=(12, 3)), rng.normal(size=12)

ev = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=LeaveOneOut(),
                     scoring="explained_variance")
r2 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=LeaveOneOut(), scoring="r2")
print(ev.mean())  # 1.0   <- perfect score on noise, silently
print(r2.mean())  # nan   <- correctly undefined
```

### Expected Results

Something that does not claim a perfect fit on a single sample. Matching
`r2_score` seems most consistent: emit `UndefinedMetricWarning` and return `nan`
when `n_samples < 2`, since the metric is not defined without variance to
explain.

### Actual Results

```
1.0        # explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]) -- no warning
nan        # r2_score([1.0], [2.0]) -- UndefinedMetricWarning

1.0        # LeaveOneOut + explained_variance on pure noise
nan        # LeaveOneOut + r2 on pure noise (12 UndefinedMetricWarnings)
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.14
Python dependencies:
    sklearn: 1.9.0
```

### Notes

I appreciate that ignoring a systematic offset is intentional for this metric
(the docstring notes it), so the `n_samples >= 2` behaviour is not in question
here — only the single-sample case, where there is no variance at all and the
score is silently reported as perfect.

I'm happy to open a PR adding the same `n_samples < 2` guard that `r2_score`
already uses, if that's the direction you'd prefer.
issues.author: PranavAchar01

comments.body:
One clarification after looking at the existing coverage, since it affects how deliberate the current behaviour is.

`test_regression_metrics_at_limits` does pin the single-sample case:

```python

# Note: for r2 and d2_tweedie see also test_regression_single_sample
...
assert_almost_equal(explained_variance_score([0.0], [0.0]), 1.0)
```

but that assertion uses `y_true == y_pred`, i.e. a **perfect** single-sample prediction, where returning `1.0` is reasonable. The case in this report is the **incorrect** single-sample prediction (`explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]) == 1.0`), which as far as I can tell is not covered by any test.

So the distinction may be narrower than "change the single-sample behaviour": the perfect case could keep returning `1.0` while a non-zero residual at `n_samples == 1` is what is arguably misreported. That said, both collapse to the same `0/0` under `force_finite`, so separating them would need an explicit `n_samples < 2` branch anyway.

I did not open a PR since the existing assertion looks intentional — happy to implement whichever direction you prefer (warn + `nan` like `r2_score`, or keep the value and document the single-sample caveat).

issues.title: SelectFromModel's `prefit` fails unless fit is called when set_output(transform="pandas")
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

My understanding is that if `prefit`is true, one could, in principle call `transform()` without calling `fit()` first.

While this is true if we don't set the output to pandas, it fails when we do so:

Minimal reproduction:

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel

X, y = load_iris(as_frame=True, return_X_y=True)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)

# prefit=True -- docs say we don't need to call .fit() on sel
sel = SelectFromModel(clf, prefit=True).set_output(transform="pandas")

sel.transform(X)
```

```
NotFittedError: This SelectFromModel instance is not fitted yet. Call 'fit' with appropriate arguments before using this estimator.
```

Without `.set_output(transform="pandas")`, the identical `prefit=True` selector transforms `X` just fine with no `.fit()` call. 

The error only appears once pandas output is requested, because `set_output` internally calls `get_feature_names_out()`, which checks whether the *wrapper itself* has been fitted (via `check_is_fitted(self)`, not `check_is_fitted(self.estimator)`). 

According to Claude, that check was intentionally added in #25308 to standardize `get_feature_names_out()` behavior across `SelectorMixin` estimators.

So my question is: is this expected behaviour? or is it an unintended bug? 

From a user perspective, if I use `fit`again, even though prefit is True, I get the impression that my estimator would be re-fitted, so if this is intended, it might be worth adding a line in the docs.

```python
sel.fit(X, y)     # with prefit=True, does NOT retrain clf -- just
                  # deep-copies it and records feature_names_in_
sel.transform(X)  # now works
```

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

SelectFromModel's prefit parameter is documented as:

prefit : bool, default=False
Whether a prefit model is expected to be passed into the constructor directly or not. If True, estimator must be a fitted estimator. If False, estimator is fitted and updated by calling fit and partial_fit, respectively.

Maybe it's just me, but I sort of read this as, if the estimator is prefit, I could avoid calling fit and it would be just fine.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a note to the prefit parameter docstring, e.g.:

Note: even with prefit=True, .fit() must still be called before using get_feature_names_out() or set_output(transform="pandas"), since these check whether the selector itself (not the underlying estimator) has been fitted. Calling .fit() in this case does not refit estimator; it only records bookkeeping metadata (estimator_, feature_names_in_).

Given the direction in the last two comments, I put together a real fix (superseding my earlier docs-only suggestion above).

Root cause: `transform()` already works with `prefit=True` before calling this meta-estimator's own `fit()`, because `_get_support_mask` falls back on `self.estimator` (`getattr(self, "estimator_", self.estimator)`) when `estimator_` hasn't been set yet. But `get_feature_names_out()` (inherited from `SelectorMixin`) always calls `check_is_fitted(self)` and `_check_feature_names_in(self, ...)`, which only look at attributes on the wrapper itself — so it raises `NotFittedError` in this case, and since `set_output(transform="pandas")` calls `get_feature_names_out()` internally to build column names, it hits the same error even though plain `transform()` works fine.

Fix: override `get_feature_names_out()` in `SelectFromModel` (not the shared `SelectorMixin`, which other selectors without `prefit` also use) to fall back on `self.estimator` for feature names/count when `estimator_` isn't set yet and `prefit=True`, mirroring `_get_support_mask`'s existing fallback. Once `fit()` has been called, it falls through to the original behavior unchanged — still needed for estimators that don't track their own feature names (`test_estimator_does_not_support_feature_names` covers that and still passes, since it's the wrapper's own `fit()` that records `feature_names_in_` in that case).

This does require updating `test_prefit_get_feature_names_out`, which asserted the old `NotFittedError` — it now checks that `get_feature_names_out()` gives the same answer before and after calling `fit()`. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The PyPI wheel bundles `libgomp.so.1.0.0-8.5.0-28.el8_10.alma.1.x86_64.debug` which is probably not what we want.

Despite scikit-learn [building in manylinux_2_28](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b2958e8ac0da5f56fe82677c2a67ed960f8d3a89/.github/workflows/wheels.yml#L100), whose [docs say](https://github.com/pypa/manylinux#manylinux_2_28-almalinux-8-based) the toolchain is GCC 14, the bundled OpenMP runtime is effectively AlmaLinux 8 / GCC 8.5-era libgomp.

Codex suggests to add this repair command around [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b2958e8ac0da5f56fe82677c2a67ed960f8d3a89/.github/workflows/wheels.yml#L194) to the linux build:

```yaml
          CIBW_REPAIR_WHEEL_COMMAND_LINUX: >
            LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rh/gcc-toolset-14/root/usr/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
            auditwheel repair -w {dest_dir} {wheel}
```

`auditwheel repair` decides which concrete shared object to copy into `scikit_learn.libs` (what is bundled in the PyPi wheel). Without help, it resolves the base AlmaLinux 8 runtime. With `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` pointing to gcc-toolset first, it should resolve to the newer gcc-toolset libgomp.

```Python
import threadpoolctl

for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
```

An issue I see with this approach is that it's kind of a hack. Basically, what we're doing here is to apply the mutations which `_validate_data` would have done to the estimator, after the fact, w/o calling `_validate_data`, or having passed data which is different from the data given by the user (like converted to an ndarray version of the data). - Disable input validation on the estimator level, for sub-estimators of `RandomForest`, so that `rf.estimators_[0].predict(df)` doesn't call validation and doesn't raise/warn anything.
- Or, have a protocol where `_validate_data` tells us what mutations it's doing, and apply the same thing on sub-estimators.

> What was the thinking behind the current "early conversion" approach?

1. Performance: Validation and multiple conversion can be VERY expensive. Worst case we'd have a whole data copy when converting to ndarray every time. That's also why we have things like this in the meta-estimator level:
```py
        if issparse(X):
            # Pre-sort indices to avoid that each individual tree of the
            # ensemble sorts the indices.
```

2. In some cases we need to know certain information about the input already in the meta-estimator level, which can be avoided in the `BaseForest` case it seems, but the performance reason stands. We do bootstrapping there, but we can do it w/o conversion, which probably would be more expensive too.

So we can only _delay_ validation when:
1. we don't need info / modifications on the input
2. we only fit one sub-estimator, so we won't have the issue of multiple validations

issues.title: Improve error message when a polars `LazyFrame` is passed to `check_array`
issues.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Passing a polars `LazyFrame` to `check_array` — e.g. the result of
`pl.scan_parquet(...)` without a final `.collect()` — produces an error that suggests
reshaping the input. Through an estimator (`StandardScaler().fit(lazy_frame)`) the
error is different but equally unhelpful: `ValueError: setting an array element with
a sequence.`. Neither message mentions the `LazyFrame` or the actionable fix, which
is to call `.collect()`. An eager `pl.DataFrame` works fine; only the lazy variant
fails, so this is easy to hit at the end of a polars `scan_*` pipeline and the
reshape advice sends the user in the wrong direction.

(Lazy-frame *support* was discussed in the narwhals adoption RFC #31049 and left
out of scope — the expression-API code path that would enable it was not favored,
and row order is undefined on a narwhals `LazyFrame`. This issue is only about
failing with a useful message.)

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import polars as pl
from sklearn.utils import check_array
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_lazy = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1.0, 2.0], "b": [3.0, 4.0]})

check_array(X_lazy)            # ValueError: Expected 2D array, got scalar array ...
StandardScaler().fit(X_lazy)   # ValueError: setting an array element with a sequence.
```

### Expected Results

An error that names the type and the fix, in the same spirit as the existing
`np.matrix` and sparse-input guards:

```
TypeError: A polars LazyFrame was passed, but lazy dataframes are not supported. Use '.collect()' to convert it to a polars DataFrame.
```

### Actual Results

```
ValueError: Expected 2D array, got scalar array instead:
array=naive plan: (run LazyFrame.explain(optimized=True) to see the optimized plan)

DF ["a", "b"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS.
Reshape your data either using array.reshape(-1, 1) if your data has a single feature or array.reshape(1, -1) if it contains a single sample.
```

Through an estimator instead of `check_array` directly:

```
ValueError: setting an array element with a sequence.
```

The `LazyFrame` is not recognized by the narwhals-based dataframe detection
(`nw.dependencies.is_into_dataframe` returns `False` for it) and falls through to
`np.asarray`, which wraps it as a 0-d object scalar — hence the misleading messages
with the stringified query plan in the middle.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.5 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Jun 12 2025, 11:23:37) [Clang 14.0.6 ]
   machine: macOS-15.7.3-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
          pip: None
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.4.6
        scipy: 1.17.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.22.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

polars 1.41.2. Also reproduced on the `1.10.dev0` nightly wheel (current main).


### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would like to work on a PR (I will wait for triage before opening it).

Root cause: `check_array` detects dataframes via
`nw.dependencies.is_into_dataframe` / `is_into_series`, both of which return
`False` for a `LazyFrame`, so it falls through to `np.asarray`, which wraps the
`LazyFrame` as a 0-d object scalar. The downstream dimension checks then produce
the misleading "scalar array" / "setting an array element with a sequence" errors.

Proposed fix: add an early guard in `check_array`, next to the narwhals dataframe
handling, using `narwhals.stable.v2.dependencies.is_polars_lazyframe` (available at
the current `narwhals>=2.0.1` floor), raising a `TypeError` that names the type and
suggests `.collect()`, following the wording style of the existing `np.matrix` and
sparse-input guards. The guard would be polars-specific: the generic
`is_into_lazyframe` helper is not available at the narwhals version floor, and the
`.collect()` advice is polars-specific anyway. I have this implemented locally with
tests and a changelog fragment.
